topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Lenses
target_audience: University students (Linear Algebra) or advanced High School students

outline.topic: Change of Basis: Seeing the World Through Different Lenses
outline.target_audience: University students (Linear Algebra) or advanced High School students

sections.title: The Hook: Two Perspectives, One Truth
sections.content: Introduce the idea that the same physical point can be described by different sets of numbers depending on your coordinate system. Use a scenario where two characters use different 'ruling' systems.
sections.example: An Arctic Explorer (using a standard North-East grid) and a Penguin (using a grid aligned with the slope of an iceberg) are both looking at a fish. The Explorer says it's at (3, 2), but the Penguin says it's at (1, 4). Who is right? Both are!

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
sections.content: Briefly review that a basis is a set of linearly independent vectors that 'span' the space. Visually show the standard basis vectors i-hat (1,0) and j-hat (0,1).
sections.example: Graphically show a standard 2D grid. Highlight that (3,2) means 3 steps of i-hat and 2 steps of j-hat. This is the 'Standard Basis'.

sections.title: The Concept: Defining a New Language
sections.content: Introduce a second basis (Basis B). Explain that to 'translate' between the Explorer and the Penguin, we need to know how the Penguin’s unit vectors look in the Explorer’s world.
sections.example: Visual: The Penguin's grid is tilted 45 degrees. We represent the Penguin's first unit vector b1 and second vector b2 as arrows within the Explorer's standard grid.

sections.title: The 'Translator' Matrix (Change of Basis Matrix)
sections.content: Show how to construct the Change of Basis Matrix [P]. The columns of this matrix are simply the coordinates of the new basis vectors (Penguin's units) written in terms of the old basis (Explorer's units).
sections.example: If the Penguin's 'step' b1 is (1, 1) in the Explorer's world and b2 is (-1, 1), the Change of Basis Matrix P has these as its columns: [[1, -1], [1, 1]].

sections.title: The Transformation Formula
sections.content: Explain the mathematical operation: [Vector in Old Basis] = [P] * [Vector in New Basis]. Emphasize that the matrix P acts as a 'bridge' or 'map' between the two coordinate languages.
sections.example: If the Penguin says the fish is at (2, 1) in his system, we multiply P by [2, 1] to find that the Explorer sees the fish at (1, 3). The animation shows the Penguin's grid lines 'stretching and rotating' to match the Explorer's grid.

sections.title: The Reverse Gear: Inverse Matrix
sections.content: Briefly explain how to go the other way. If we want to translate the Explorer's view back to the Penguin's, we use the inverse of matrix P (P^-1).
sections.example: A Drone (Device) sends coordinates to the Explorer. To help the Penguin find the location, the Explorer multiplies the coordinates by the inverse matrix P^-1 to speak the 'Penguin language'.

sections.title: Summary and Visual Wrap-up
sections.content: Recap the core idea: A change of basis doesn't move the vector; it just changes the description. Summarize the steps: 1. Find new basis vectors in old terms. 2. Build the Matrix P. 3. Multiply to translate.
sections.example: Final animation: A split-screen showing the same vector while the background grid swaps between 'Standard' and 'Alternative' bases, highlighting that the arrow itself remains stationary.

storyboard.title: The Hook: Two Perspectives, One Truth
lecture_lines: One point, two different numerical descriptions.
The Explorer sees the fish at (3, 2).
The Penguin sees the same fish at (1, 4).
animations: Fade in a blue (#0000FF) dot at (3, 2) on a black background.
Fade in a white (#FFFFFF) standard grid representing the Explorer's view.
Label the dot with coordinates (3, 2) in white (#FFFFFF).
Overlay a yellow (#FFFF00) tilted grid representing the Penguin's view.
Change the coordinate label to (1, 4) in yellow (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: What is a Basis?
lecture_lines: A basis is a set of spanning vectors.
Standard basis uses unit vectors i-hat and j-hat.
Coordinates are just weights for these basis vectors.
animations: Display a white (#FFFFFF) standard grid with origin (0,0).
Draw green (#00FF00) i-hat and red (#FF0000) j-hat basis vectors.
Show the vector (3, 2) as 3 * i-hat + 2 * j-hat.

storyboard.title: The Concept: Defining a New Language
lecture_lines: The Penguin uses her own tilted coordinate system.
We describe her units using the Explorer's grid.
This sets the stage for a mathematical translation.
animations: Draw a standard grid with cyan (#00FFFF) b1 and magenta (#FF00FF) b2 arrows.
Display coordinates b1 = (1, 1) and b2 = (-1, 1) as labels.
Highlight b1 and b2 as the new basis vectors for the Penguin.

storyboard.title: The 'Translator' Matrix (Change of Basis Matrix)
lecture_lines: The Change of Basis Matrix P is our translator.
First column: Penguin's first basis vector in standard terms.
Second column: Penguin's second basis vector in standard terms.
Matrix P columns are the new basis vectors.
This matrix maps the Penguin's world to ours.
animations: Show coordinates of b1 (1,1) and b2 (-1,1) on screen.
Display an orange (#FFA500) 2x2 matrix P with empty slots.
Move b1's coordinates into the first column of matrix P.
Move b2's coordinates into the second column of matrix P.
Highlight the final matrix P = [[1, -1], [1, 1]] in orange.

storyboard.title: The Transformation Formula
lecture_lines: Multiply P by the Penguin's vector coordinates.
The result is the vector in the Explorer's basis.
This transformation formula acts as a coordinate bridge.
Watch the Penguin's grid transform into the Explorer's.
The matrix converts descriptions between different bases.
animations: Show the equation [x]_standard = P * [x]_penguin in white (#FFFFFF).
Substitute P with the matrix and [x]_penguin with vector [2, 1].
Animate the step-by-step matrix-vector multiplication.
Show the resulting vector (1, 3) on the standard grid.
Animate the Penguin's grid morphing into the Explorer's standard grid.

storyboard.title: The Reverse Gear: Inverse Matrix
lecture_lines: Use the inverse matrix P-inverse to go back.
It translates the Explorer's coordinates into the Penguin's.
Matrix inversion provides the reverse translation path.
animations: Introduce the inverse matrix P^-1 in light blue (#ADD8E6).
Show the formula [x]_penguin = P^-1 * [x]_standard in light blue.
Animate the conversion of Explorer's (1, 3) back to Penguin's (2, 1).

storyboard.title: Summary and Visual Wrap-up
lecture_lines: Changing basis doesn't move the physical vector.
It only changes the labels we use.
Build matrix P using the new basis vectors.
Multiply to switch between different coordinate languages.
Different lenses, but the same geometric truth.
animations: Show a single vector arrow stationary on a black background.
Switch the background grid between Standard (white) and Penguin (yellow).
Display the summary: 'Same vector, different basis, different coordinates'.
